cells.tense: This is arriving now and you are letting it land in its own time.
cells.ask: Name one person you feel with rather than only about, tell them what you noticed, and let their answer stand as it comes.
cells.core: Something near you is asking to be felt with, and you're letting it land. You can be moved by what someone's going through without the edges going soft. You still know where you end. That's the part that's easy to miss, because a room usually rewards one side or the other: stay untouched, or go all the way in. You're doing neither. You're close enough to feel it and clear enough to say what you see. When the person across from you is carrying something hard, you don't take it from them and you don't step back into safety. You stay in contact and hold your own shape. That kind of presence is quiet. Most of it goes unnamed. But it's what lets the next thing arrive without the whole room tilting.
cells.sheetLine: You feel with people and still keep your own edges.
cells.verb: to feel with what is near, without losing the edge between you
cells.place: at the door where what was outside is crossing in

cells.tense: You will have taken on the room's mood before any of it has even arrived.
cells.ask: Let one thing that isn't yours stay with its owner this week, and leave the room without carrying it home.
cells.core: You're ahead of what's actually here, already feeling what people haven't said yet. Somewhere just ahead there's a scene where they're fine and you're the one holding it, and you're living there before the door opens. So the edge between you and them stops holding. You pick up a mood the second you walk in. You answer a question that hasn't been asked. You carry what someone else might have carried fine alone. The feeling is genuine, which is what makes it hard to catch. It's just early, and it's reaching past where it belongs. The weight you spend yourself on hasn't arrived. Part of it won't. Part of it wasn't yours to take.
cells.sheetLine: You're feeling a mood that hasn't reached you yet.

cells.tense: You stopped letting anyone over the threshold some time back, and the room has been quiet since.
cells.ask: Tell one person a true thing about how this week sits with you, then stay in the conversation for two minutes of what comes back.
cells.core: People come near and stop at the surface. It isn't that you're cold. You got careful, and careful became the whole room. Now conversations stay polite and you're not really in them. Someone tells you something that matters and part of you stays outside it, watching. Contact doesn't happen to you; it happens near you. The feeling isn't gone — it's behind a closed latch, and pressing at the feeling won't open it. What opens it is smaller. One honest sentence to one person, said out loud where they can answer. Not a revelation. Just enough of the real thing to let them in, and you close the door again if you like.
cells.sheetLine: People come close and stop at the surface. You've been letting them.
cells.verb: to feel with what is near, without losing the edge between you

cells.tense: People are already feeling held by you while you call it keeping the peace.
cells.ask: Say one thing out loud that shows you noticed what someone is going through, and don't explain why you said it.
cells.core: People leave conversations with you feeling met. You're the reason several of them are steadier than they walked in. You'd say you were just being polite. Look at what you actually do: you wait a beat longer before answering. You remember what someone said last week and ask about it. You sit down next to the person standing alone. That's pattern, not manners. It's the same thing you do at each table, and it's why people tell you things they don't tell other people. You see the shape of what's going on for someone and you act on it without calling it anything. It runs while you're not looking. You just haven't taken it as yours. The one person who gets no credit for it is you.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the compassion is already arriving from somewhere and the person is refusing it — the record says the seat is what is entering, but nothing says the person has put a door in front of it; a reader could reasonably say they never asked for it to arrive and would rather be left alone, which the record does not cover. The ask survives being wrong because naming one person does not require the recognition to be real: naming is a claim the person can make with nothing behind it, so it still gives them a move if the read misses. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line describing the other person's feeling — it would make the reading sound deep while telling the person what their friend experiences, which they cannot confirm and did not come for.
